l: Integrating retrieval-augmented generation for enhanced personalized physician recommendations in web-based medical services: model development study
s: This Frontiers in Public Health article by Yingbin Zheng, Yiwei Yan, Sai Chen, Yunping Cai, Kun Ren, Yishan Liu, Jiaying Zhuang, and Min Zhao develops and evaluates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation-Based Physician Recommendation (RAGPR) model for web-based medical services. It addresses the difficulty of matching patients to suitable physicians through personalized recommendations, contrasting RAG with manual triage, symptom checkers, decision trees, rule-based systems, collaborative filtering, and content-based filtering. The study uses 646,383 anonymized consultation records from the Internet Hospital of the First Affiliated Hospital of Xiamen University, covering 193,675 patients, 858 physicians, and 44 departments, plus 965 web-based medical documents from Hugging Face for testing. RAGPR embeds documents with Sentence-BERT, stores them in Chroma, retrieves six relevant queries using Maximal Marginal Relevance, and uses a locally constructed LLaMA-based large language model to generate department and physician recommendations. The authors assess performance with precision, recall, F1-score, and ratings by three triage staff members. The results compare FastText, SBERT, and OpenAI embeddings: OpenAI has the highest classification metrics, but SBERT is chosen for implementation because it balances performance with cost, data security, and ease of migration. Mistral, GPT-4o-mini, and GPT-4o are compared for recommendations. GPT-4o achieves the highest F1-score, while Mistral is selected as a practical, rational option. A case study indicates that RAGPR can infer relevant specialties from symptom descriptions and recommend corresponding departments and physicians. The discussion presents RAGPR as a means to improve the accuracy and efficiency of web-based consultation triage. It emphasizes implementation needs including infrastructure, staff training, privacy, interoperability, bias mitigation, and ongoing updating. Limitations are its single-hospital evaluation, irrelevant dataset questions, and limited transparency; proposed future work includes real-time data, multimodal inputs, and explainable models. The study was ethics-approved by the First Affiliated Hospital of Xiamen University Ethics Committee, used deidentified data, and reports no conflicts of interest.

l: TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: This document is the paper “TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text,” by Songshuo Lu, Hua Wang, Yutian Rong, Zhi Chen, and Yaohua Tang of Moore Threads AI, published in the Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. It addresses the online prefill cost and time-to-first-token (TTFT) bottleneck in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), where a large language model uses retrieved external documents to answer questions. TurboRAG uses a hybrid offline-online design: it precomputes key-value caches for document chunks offline, retrieves those caches at inference, and stitches them into a contextual cache rather than recomputing retrieved text. Independent Attention prevents cross-attention among document chunks, while Composite Positions and Reordered Positions address RoPE positional encoding when chunks are concatenated or reordered. The reordered approach applies RoPE at inference with negligible added cost. Lightweight supervised fine-tuning adapts the model to the new attention masks and position handling, then inference retrieves documents, forms the cache, prefills the model, and generates an answer. The paper situates TurboRAG among approaches that shorten retrieved text, accelerate decoding, reuse or compress caches, and optimize attention; it presents TurboRAG as complementary to cache compression, speculative decoding, prefix caching, and decoding-kernel optimization. Experiments compare Naïve RAG, TurboRAG variants, and GPT-4o-2024-08-06 on RGB and LongBench document question answering, general capabilities, TTFT, and batch scaling. Fine-tuned models retain broadly comparable accuracy, with TurboRAG-reordered generally stronger than TurboRAG-composite. Reported LongBench average TTFT reduction is 8.6×, up to 9.4× in the main results; Qwen-2 results reach 11.23× for the 72B model. Tested batch scaling shows about 98.46% fewer TFLOPs than Naïve RAG, and advantages persist as batch size grows. Supplementary material gives positional-encoding pseudocode, fine-tuning data proportions, an RGB example, LLaMA-3.1-8B results across noise ratios, and FLOPS calculations. The conclusion emphasizes reduced online computation but notes storage, memory, distributed deployment, dynamic knowledge bases, and continued fine-tuning as limitations; KV-cache compression is proposed as an orthogonal future direction.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a generation framework and method that couples a dense retriever and a large language model, using external knowledge to ground generation. It is a de-facto solution for knowledge-intensive NLP tasks and has documented gains for question answering, code synthesis, and creative writing. Conventionally, it retrieves many document chunks, concatenates them, and prefills them for generation. This design can require substantial online computation, increase time-to-first-token, recompute redundant work, incur quadratic prefill cost, and restrict batch size. Work on accelerating it has reduced retrieved text or decoding cost and reused caches under strict ordering. TurboRAG instead aggregates retrieved document fragments through concatenated pre-computed KV caches. In document-QA and long-context comparisons with Naïve RAG, TurboRAG variants preserve RAG accuracy while reducing inference latency and computation. Its discussion suggests direct query-document interactions can often suffice without expensive cross-attention between fragments.

l: KV cache, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: KV cache is a stored key and value representation and cache used in language model inference for subsequent attention computation. In TurboRAG, it is computed offline for each document or passage chunk, stored in a database or on disk, and later retrieved for relevant text. Online, retrieved chunk caches are loaded from storage to GPU and concatenated or stitched, using reordered positional semantics, for generation; this avoids recomputing frequently retrieved chunks during each conventional RAG query and reduces long-text online computation. A 512-token Qwen2-7B chunk has a 28 MB FP16 cache, so one million such chunks require about 28 TB of disk. Storage and loading therefore create deployment pressure, though quantization, compression, selective eviction, merging, and GPU prefetching can reduce footprint or communication overhead. In the described pipeline, key_states and value_states are maintained through past_key_value, with RoPE-related values included in cache_kwargs.

s: Chunked text is identified as the text format for which TurboRAG uses precomputed KV caches.

l: standard RAG, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: Standard RAG retrieves top document chunks for a query, concatenates them, and performs one online prefill to build a KV cache before autoregressive generation. Processing the full context creates significant TTFT latency and resource use. TurboRAG addresses this overhead without changing models or inference systems, reporting up to 9.4× lower TTFT without compromising accuracy.

l: TurboRAG, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: TurboRAG is a hybrid offline–online retrieval-augmented generation framework for latency-optimized large-language-model use. Offline, it precomputes and stores chunk- or passage-level key-value caches. At inference time, it retrieves relevant caches and stitches or concatenates them rather than performing online prefill computation for the retrieved content. This stitching uses Independent Attention, which masks cross-chunk or inter-document attention, and reordered, RoPE-consistent positions, with position IDs reordered into monotone increasing numbers within chunks. These techniques support order-agnostic cache stitching while preserving positional semantics. The system is intended for most existing large language models without changing model architecture or inference systems, although its pipeline uses lightweight supervised fine-tuning so a model can consume the new cache layout and attention setting. Its reported goal and main result are sharply reduced time to first token while retaining accuracy comparable to conventional or Naïve RAG. Reported reductions include up to 9.4× TTFT improvement, 8.6× on average, about 98.5% lower online GPU resource use, and 98.46% fewer TFLOPs in a batch-scaling experiment. With host-to-device transfer, reported speedups range from 4.1× at batch size 1 to 4.7× at batch size 6. Reduced resource use also increases supported batch size. TurboRAG is evaluated on LongBench multi-document QA benchmarks. It can complement retrieval sparsification, cache compression, speculative decoding, cross-request prefix caching, and decoding-phase attention optimization. Its positional-encoding options include Composite Positions and Reordered Positions. From setup through inference, it shifts document-cache computation offline, retrieves and joins caches online with modified masks and positions, then generates with lower prefill latency. Its stated trade-off is increased storage space and memory pressure, and the current pipeline still requires fine-tuning.

l: retrieved document chunks, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: TurboRAG is a pipeline that handles retrieved document chunks by computing and storing each chunk’s KV cache independently offline, then reusing and combining caches across queries without cross-attention. This avoids conventional concatenation before prefill and its O(k) input-length growth for k chunks.

l: prefill computation, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: Prefill computation computes a KV cache for an entire concatenated document set online and is a critical generation-pipeline bottleneck. As chunks are added, conventional prefill repeats work and incurs quadratic cost. TurboRAG shifts chunk-level cache computation offline, then loads and reuses precomputed passage caches online, reducing or eliminating retrieved-content prefill time.

l: TTFT, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: TTFT is a metric, measured in milliseconds, for time to first token in RAG comparisons. It matters because conventional RAG’s processing of many retrieved document chunks increases it, while TurboRAG substantially reduces it. Reported results begin with up to a 9.4× reduction and an 8.6× average reduction on LongBench; the advantage remains substantial or grows with larger batches and contexts. In Qwen-2 measurements, speedups range from 2.31× to 11.23×. One comparison lists TTFT falling from 87 for Naïve RAG to 36 for TurboRAG, and an on-device scenario keeps it below one second.

l: large language model, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: The large language model is a large language model used to process retrieved context and generate outputs, serving as the generator in Retrieval–Augmented Generation. It computes queries, keys, values, attention scores, hidden states, and KV caches during prefill and autoregressive decoding; its per-token cost spans layers and is characterized by L, H, K, dh, d, and dmlp. It employs Swiglu and can adapt to varied positional embeddings. In TurboRAG, it is coupled with a dense retriever and lightly supervised fine-tuned to consume a new cache layout, attention mask matrix, position embeddings, and concatenated document KV caches without question-answering accuracy regression. Its flexibility supports this approach, but TurboRAG’s fine-tuning dependency prevents direct application to newly emerging state-of-the-art large language models.

s: evaluate TurboRAG [as a suite of benchmarks] RAG benchmarks are used to evaluate TurboRAG across a suite of tasks. The experimental results show substantial time-to-first-token reductions compared with conventional RAG systems.

l: answer quality, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: TurboRAG preserves answer quality, achieving performance comparable to standard RAG systems.

l: document, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: This document describes TurboRAG’s handling of external documents: documents, possibly unrelated to a question, are enclosed by markers, encoded as embeddings for vector similarity search, and prefetched offline by an LLM so their KV caches can later be retrieved and combined for a query.

l: Independent Attention, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: Independent Attention is a TurboRAG inference method motivated by typically negligible inter-chunk attention and documents’ focus on internal information. It prevents attention between document chunks, letting each document attend only to itself, while the query and generated answer attend to all documents by simulating retrieval and concatenation of separately computed KV caches.

l: position IDs, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: Position IDs determine indices for position embeddings. Naively stitched caches can give inconsistent IDs and degrade accuracy. TurboRAG begins with repeated per-chunk ranges, reorders cached document-key IDs into standard monotone increasing, contiguous indices, and aligns positional differences with locations in concatenated context.

l: RoPE, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: RoPE is a position embedding method that encodes relative pair-wise offsets, making absolute token indices irrelevant. It applies position IDs independently to queries and keys, so their interaction depends on positional difference. This supports rearranging IDs when chunk-level caches are stitched: RoPE is applied during key-value-cache precomputation in Composite Positions, then reapplied to cached or stitched key_states with new indices at inference time in Reordered Positions.

l: GPU, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: Long concatenated contexts consume substantial GPU memory in standard RAG, limiting per-device batch size and throughput. TurboRAG reduces online resource utilization and is presented as useful on devices with modest, heavily time-shared GPUs.

l: LongBench, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: LongBench is a bilingual, multitask benchmark for long-context understanding, including multi-document question answering. It evaluates long-text and multi-document RAG: TurboRAG results report comparable accuracy to baseline or Naïve RAG while reducing average TTFT from 1165 ms to 134 ms, up to 9.4× improvement.

l: multi-document question answering, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: Multi-document question answering is the evaluation setting for the reported TurboRAG experiments. The results indicate substantial TTFT improvements without compromising accuracy.

l: SFT, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: SFT is the lightweight supervised fine-tuning process used by TurboRAG to adapt a base large language model to its independent-mask, reordered-position cache layout. It replaces standard SFT attention masks and position embeddings with those required for cache-concatenation inference. TurboRAG trains Qwen2-7B models on an equal mix of document-QA and general-task data, using AdamW, 32 NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs, batch size 256, and about 888 GPU-hours.

l: cache reuse, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: Cache reuse is presented as a branch of RAG acceleration. TurboRAG advances cache reuse by enabling passage-cache stitching without dependence on passage order, while Marconi can provide complementary cross-request prefix caching.

l: KV cache compression, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: KV cache compression, an optimization technique orthogonal to TurboRAG, effectively reduces storage requirements and latency pressure; integrating it into TurboRAG is a future direction.

l: attention mask matrix, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: is_a masking matrix [used to prevent attention to future tokens] The attention mask matrix controls which tokens can attend to other tokens. TurboRAG replaces the usual lower triangular masking behavior between document chunks with a pattern that blocks cross-attention among chunks while allowing the query and answer to attend to all documents.

l: composite positions, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: Composite positions are a position-ID arrangement and TurboRAG approach for positional encodings. RoPE is applied while each chunk’s key-value cache is precomputed, making implementation straightforward. When per-document caches are concatenated without changing IDs, repeated ranges such as [0, ..., l, 0, ..., l] result, whose positional differences mismatch actual token-index differences.

l: reordered positions, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: Reordered positions is an approach for handling positional encodings in TurboRAG’s concatenated key caches. It assigns contiguous indices across document chunks so cached-key positional differences match original token offsets. During inference, it applies RoPE to stitched key_states using apply_single_rotary_pos_emb, with negligible additional cost.

s: is_encoded_by Bert [using the same encoder as documents] The user query is encoded into a vector using the same BERT-based model used for document encoding. That vector is used to retrieve relevant documents, after which the query is processed with the combined contextual KV cache.

l: answer, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: An answer is generated autoregressively after online KV cache prefill, attending to the query, prior answer tokens, and retrieved documents; it should be accurate when documents contain the correct answer and otherwise refuse to answer.

l: attention, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: Attention is a mechanism used by transformers. It compares a current generated token’s query with context keys using scaled dot products, masks and normalizes the scores, then computes the current output as a weighted sum of context value vectors; cross-attention between retrieved fragments may be unnecessary.

l: prefill, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: computes KV cache [for each document offline] Prefill computes the hidden states and KV representations for the context before response generation. TurboRAG performs document prefill offline and performs another online prefill using the combined document caches and the input query.

l: document question-answering, TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text
s: Document question-answering is a 50% fine-tuning data task using English and Chinese datasets. Because TurboRAG’s new attention mask matrix and position embeddings may reduce accuracy, TurboRAG fine-tunes the LLM. Evaluations on RGB Benchmark and LongBench, across retrieved, long-context, noisy, and multi-document settings, show fine-tuned models generally match Naïve RAG, with TurboRAG-reordered strongest.

s: retrieves document [the most relevant documents from the vector database] Similarity search compares the encoded user query with stored document embeddings. It retrieves the most relevant documents whose KV caches are then used to form the online contextual cache.

s: TurboRAG inference pipeline is a process that encodes documents offline, stores embeddings and KV caches in a vector index, retrieves relevant documents for a query through similarity search, concatenates their caches, performs online prefill, and generates an answer.

s: Naïve RAG is a conventional retrieval-augmented generation system and the baseline used throughout experiments for comparison with TurboRAG. In Table 10, it has 743 context tokens, 87 ms TTFT, and 2.42x speedup. It matches or slightly exceeds TurboRAG on some accuracy measures, but has substantially higher TTFT and computational load, particularly with long contexts and larger batches. Its RGB averages are 97.1 in Chinese and 98.4 in English; its RGB Information Integration Task averages are 51.7 in Chinese and 62.3 in English. It remains robust without fine-tuning at RGB noise ratio 0.8, then after fine-tuning keeps its accuracy gap within 1% of Naïve RAG. It matches Naïve RAG on LongBench and generalizes across OpenCompass without significant degradation. On LLaMA-3.1-8B, it averages 95.0 in Chinese RGB and 97.4 in English RGB, while RGB Information Integration averages are 48.3 and 62.0. It also delivers an average 8.6x TTFT speedup on LongBench.

l: GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: This is an ACL 2025 paper, “GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation,” by Zhili Shen and colleagues at Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd. It presents GEAR, a retrieval-augmented generation framework for open-domain multi-hop question answering, where answering requires evidence from several passages. The paper’s central components are SyncGE, a graph-enhanced retriever, and an agentic multi-step retrieval process with memory, answer assessment, and query rewriting. GEAR represents passages through associated triples: each triple is linked to one passage, while passages may contain multiple triples. A large language model summarizes retrieved passages into proximal triples, connects them to a triple graph, and uses Diverse Triple Beam Search with a generic semantic model to expand multiple relevant paths. This avoids repeatedly prompting an LLM to traverse the graph. Across iterations, GEAR stores a gist memory of the multi-hop context, determines whether the evidence can answer the original question, and, if necessary, rewrites the query for further retrieval. When it terminates, it maps memorized triples back to passages and fuses these with previously retrieved passages through Reciprocal Rank Fusion. The paper situates GEAR against query-expansion, iterative retrieval-and-prompting, offline-indexing, and graph-based systems such as IRCoT, GraphReader, TRACE, and HippoRAG, arguing that existing approaches can face issues with updates, filtering, predefined concepts, or semantic relationships. Experiments on MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and 2Wiki-MultiHopQA use Recall@5, Recall@10, Recall@15, Exact Match, and F1. GEAR reports state-of-the-art multi-step retrieval, including R@15 of 71.5 on MuSiQue, 95.9 on 2Wiki-MultiHopQA, and 97.3 on HotpotQA, with gains exceeding 10% on MuSiQue. It also achieves the best listed end-to-end QA EM and F1 using five passages. Analysis finds that SyncGE improves all tested base retrievers, diverse triple beams outperform standard beam search, and retrieval recall positively correlates with QA performance. GEAR is especially effective for low-to-moderate-complexity questions and uses fewer iterations and LLM tokens than HippoRAG w/ IRCoT. The paper closes by noting possible improvements in entity disambiguation, knowledge graph completion, triple scoring, gist memory, reasoning, and query rewriting.

l: GEAR, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: GEAR, short for Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation, is a system and novel graph-enhanced retrieval-agent framework for retrieving passages that enable retrieval-augmented models to answer multi-hop queries. It advances Retrieval-augmented Generation through two linked elements: an efficient graph expansion mechanism and an agent framework for multi-step retrieval. Offline, it aligns passages with extracted triples to create interconnected indices. During retrieval, its graph-based passage component, SyncGE, returns multi-hop contexts. GEAR turns these contexts into gist memory, proximal triples associated with passages, to maintain and summarize knowledge across steps. The agent models multi-step information seeking: it reads multi-hop contexts, maintains gist memory, assesses answerability, rewrites queries when needed, and terminates by returning one ranked passage list. Its central claim is that synchronising graph retrieval with the large language model makes multi-step retrieval more effective and efficient: it requires fewer iterations and fewer LLM tokens than other iterative retrieval methods, including HippoRAG w/ IRCoT even with a single iteration. Evaluated on MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and 2WikiMultihopQA against IRCoT, HippoRAG w/ IRCoT, and single-step approaches, GEAR achieves state-of-the-art multi-step retrieval results across the reported datasets. Reported R@15 scores are 71.5 on MuSiQue, 95.9 on 2Wiki-MultiHopQA, and 97.3 on HotpotQA; it also reports 93.4, 96.8, and 97.3 recall at R@5, R@10, and R@15 on HotpotQA. On MuSiQue, it delivers gains above 10%, a 21% relative R@15 improvement, and 37% relative improvements in both EM and F1 versus HippoRAG w/ IRCoT. In end-to-end QA using the top five passages, it has the highest EM and F1 scores across MuSiQue, 2Wiki, and HotpotQA. It is particularly strong on low-to-moderate-complexity questions, handles 3-hop questions with enhanced capability, and remains consistent across chunks with differing triple densities.

s: Multi-hop retrieval scenarios are challenging for traditional sparse and dense retrievers. GEAR is designed to improve retrieval in these scenarios.

l: graph expansion mechanism, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: GEAR is an efficient graph expansion mechanism augmenting conventional retrievers like BM25, shown effective, with graph construction improvements potentially further enhancing it.

l: graph-enhanced framework of retrieval agent, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: GEAR is a graph-enhanced retrieval agent framework that integrates graph-based retrieval into multi-step retrieval to retrieve passages relevant to multi-hop queries.

l: graph-based retrieval, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: GEAR’s agent framework integrates graph-based retrieval into multi-step retrieval, using graph expansion for each query to obtain relevant passages through termination and query-rewriting stages.

l: multi-step retrieval framework, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: The multi-step retrieval framework receives graph-based retrieval through GEAR's agent framework.

l: MuSiQue, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: MuSiQue is a challenging open-domain multi-hop question answering dataset, with 3-hop questions and questions grouped by triple density in golden passages. It is used with IRCoT-provided data and full corpus. In evaluations, it is one of three benchmarks for retrieval and question answering, where GEAR reports gains exceeding 10% and Recall@5/10/15 of 58.4/67.6/71.5. For end-to-end QA, GEAR reaches 19.0 EM and 35.6 F1, above Hybrid + SyncGE’s 14.0 EM and 27.1 F1. GEAR is especially strong on 2-hop and 3-hop questions in a single iteration.

l: large language model, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: The large language model is a component of GEAR and SyncGE for retrieval-augmented question answering. It receives relevant passages, reads passages and queries, summarizes knowledge triples, locates initial triples and nodes, and guides graph expansion. During GEAR’s multi-step process, it produces proximal triples, determines answerability, supplies reasoning, rewrites queries, and links gist-memory triples with multi-hop passages. From initial retrieval through synchronized graph reasoning and termination, it supports gist-memory construction, improved retrieval, and fewer tokens than HippoRAG w/ IRCoT.

l: Question Answering, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: Question Answering is a task evaluated by Exact Match and F1 score. Retrieval-augmented Generation enhances it, while multi-hop QA requires reasoning across several passages or documents. The work examines retrieval-augmented and multi-hop approaches, using Appendix K.3 prompts. Results link higher retrieval recall to better performance; with five passages, GEAR leads listed retrievers on MuSiQue, 2Wiki, and HotpotQA.

l: open-domain multi-hop question answering, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: Open-domain multi-hop question answering is a complex retrieval-augmented generation challenge requiring reasoning across several passages or documents rather than one-step retrieval. It underlies MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and 2Wiki-MultiHopQA evaluation of retrieval and answering. GEAR models its information-seeking process: SyncGE retrieves and links contexts, while gist memory summarizes them across iterations.

l: graph-based approaches, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: Graph-based approaches address complex multi-hop QA reasoning by extracting entities, atomic facts, or semantic triples for direct paths, but recursive LLM graph traversal can be expensive.

l: HippoRAG, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: HippoRAG is a retrieval system that extracts semantic triples from passages offline, forms knowledge graphs, and aligns triples with passages. It uses Personalized PageRank, a PageRank variant, to retrieve passages while remaining agnostic to the triples’ semantic relationships. It operates as a single-step retriever or, with IRCoT, combines a multi-step agent with graph retrieval and improves multi-hop retrieval. Evaluations report R@15 and end-to-end QA results, while Hybrid + SyncGE and GEAR outperform it on reported measures.

l: knowledge graph, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: A knowledge graph contains interconnected triples, with shared head or tail entities defining expansion neighborhoods; it bridges corresponding passages and supports retrieval of query-relevant passages from beginning to end.

l: GraphReader, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: GraphReader is an LLM agent that uses graph-navigating operations and, offline, extracts entities and atomic facts or semantic triples from passages to construct graphs of indexed passages.

l: TRACE, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: TRACE is an offline method that extracts entities and atomic facts or semantic triples from passages. It relies on Large Language Models to iteratively select pre-filtered candidate triples, constructing reasoning chains that ground answer generation or filter retrieved results; its search space remains limited by the candidate lists for each query.

l: SyncGE, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: SyncGE is GEAR’s graph-based passage retrieval component and proposed graph retriever. It uses a large language model only to locate initial triples or nodes, then uses a generic semantic model to expand a triple sub-graph through diverse triple beams. These beams link multi-hop passages and synchronize information from passages with triples. It retrieves triples that interconnect passages returned by a base retriever, aligns expanded triples with source passages, and combines the resulting and initial passages through Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Across evaluated single-step retrieval settings, it consistently improves corresponding base retrievers and contributes to state-of-the-art performance on MuSiQue and HotpotQA. It outperforms HippoRAG in many configurations, surpasses HippoRAG with IRCoT on MuSiQue without multiple iterations and with almost 2.9 million fewer tokens, and has lower recall variation across differing triple densities or chunk triple counts.

l: graph-based passage retrieval, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: GEAR includes a graph-based passage retrieval component called SyncGE. This component supports retrieval of subsequent hops by expanding triple sub-graphs without requiring expensive LLM calls for graph exploration.

l: HotpotQA, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: HotpotQA is an open-domain multi-hop question answering dataset and one of three benchmarks used to evaluate GEAR retrieval. Under the HippoRAG setting to limit costs, GEAR reaches Recall@5/10/15 of 93.4/96.8/97.3 and 50.4 EM, 69.4 F1, exceeding Hybrid + SyncGE; Diverse Triple Beam Search further improves recall.

l: 2Wiki, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: 2WikiMultihopQA is an open-domain multi-hop question answering dataset used, with IRCoT-provided data and corpus, to evaluate retrieval and end-to-end QA. It is described as saturated yet still responsive to multi-step improvements: GEAR reports recall of 89.1/95.3/95.9 at 5/10/15 and 47.4 EM, 62.3 F1, while Diverse Triple Beam Search improves recall over standard beam search.

l: IRCoT, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: IRCoT is a multi-step retriever that interleaves retrieval and prompting so each step guides and refines the other. It proceeds through repeated retrieval and prompting steps, and is evaluated as a multi-step retrieval baseline using BM25 and ColBERTv2 on MuSiQue, 2Wiki-MultiHopQA, and HotpotQA.

l: retrieval-augmented models for QA, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: is_a research branch This research branch augments language-model inputs with relevant passages and includes query expansion and iterative retrieval-and-prompting approaches.

l: multi-hop QA using combinations of LLMs with graphical structures, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: is_a research branch This research branch combines LLMs with graphical structures to address multi-hop question answering.

l: passage, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: A passage in index C may support multiple triples; retrieved passages yield supporting triples, link expanded and memorized triples back, and are ranked for final output.

l: offline indexing, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: forms hierarchical passage summaries Offline indexing is used to form hierarchical passage summaries or to extract entities, atomic facts, and semantic triples. Its summarisation-based use makes knowledge-base updates computationally expensive because summarisation must be repeated when new data is added.

l: structured knowledge, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: Recent approaches use structured knowledge graphs to address multi-hop QA challenges with LLMs.

l: semantic triples, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: Semantic triples are extracted from passages by GraphReader, TRACE, and HippoRAG-related methods. They are used to construct graphs, select reasoning paths, or align passages for retrieval. A triple represents a unit of graph knowledge and can be linked to a proximal triple or passage. Triples serve as initial nodes, are expanded into chains through neighboring triples, and are eventually aligned with source passages.

l: graph of indexed passages, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: is_constructed_from chunks [containing the same or neighbouring entities] A graph of indexed passages can be constructed by linking chunks that contain the same or neighbouring entities.

l: reasoning chains, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: ground answer generation TRACE uses an LLM to iteratively select triples for reasoning chains that can ground answer generation or filter retrieved results. The proposed framework considers the contributions of all triple elements participating in such chains.

l: graph-based retrieval framework, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: A graph-based retrieval framework aligns passages with extracted triples, uses a small semantic model to explore multi-hop relationships, and considers all triple elements in reasoning chains to robustly associate questions with triple reasoning chains.

l: Personalized PageRank, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: retrieves passages [from aligned passages and extracted triples] Personalized PageRank is used by HippoRAG to retrieve passages based on an alignment between passages and extracted triples.

l: semantic relationships, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: belong_to extracted triples HippoRAG remains agnostic to the semantic relationships of extracted triples. The proposed framework instead uses semantic exploration of multi-hop relationships.

l: small semantic model, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: explores multi-hop relationships [within the graph-based retrieval framework] The proposed graph-based retrieval framework uses a small semantic model to explore multi-hop relationships.

l: index of passages (C), GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: is_a index C is an index containing passages c1 through cC. It is the target index from which relevant passages are to be retrieved.

l: index of triples (T), GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: is_a index T is an index containing triples t1 through tT, with each triple associated with exactly one passage in C. A passage in C can be associated with multiple triples.

l: triple, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: A preliminary schema defines each triple as subject, predicate, and object, uniquely linked to one passage.

l: input query (q), GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: The input query q is used with an index of interest R to retrieve items relevant to the query.

l: base retrieval function, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: retrieves index of interest (R) [for a given input query q; returns a ranked list of k items] The base retrieval function h_base^k(q, R) returns a ranked list of k items from R in descending order according to a retrieval score. BM25 or a conventional dense retriever can serve as this function.

l: multi-hop capabilities, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: The base retrieval function does not require multi-hop capabilities.

l: retrieval-augmented model, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: The retrieval-augmented model uses relevant passages to answer multi-hop queries, fulfilling its stated intended purpose.

l: multi-hop queries, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: Multi-hop queries require retrieved passages for a retrieval-augmented model to answer, involve multiple information needs, and are evaluated across hop types and complexities using diversity-oriented retrieval.

l: Diverse Triple Beam Search, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: Diverse Triple Beam Search is a method for expanding initial triples into reasoning chains while retaining the top beam-size sequences. It scores triples with a dense embedding model, considers only neighbouring triples, avoids previously visited triples, and maps triples to source passages. Position-based diversity weighting promotes diversity across beams and aligns language modelling with information-retrieval objectives for multiple information needs in multi-hop queries. It consistently outperforms standard beam search across reported datasets and recall ranks; natural language inference is a possible alternative scoring function.

l: multi-step extension, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: is_a agentic framework [for multi-turn interactions with the graph-enhanced retriever] The multi-step extension models an iterative information-seeking process in which the original question is decomposed into simpler queries. At each step, it retrieves passages, updates gist memory, assesses answerability, and either terminates or produces another query.

l: gist memory, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: Gist memory is an agent component that stores proximal triples as aggregated evidence from completed retrievals. Initially empty, it updates each iteration and supports summarising information, later reading and reasoning, query re-writing, termination, and final passage-linking operations using commonly validated practices.

l: knowledge synchronisation, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: Knowledge synchronisation is a process that uses a large language model to read initial retrieved passages and a query, produce supporting proximal triples, and link each to a graph triple to identify initial nodes for graph expansion.

l: reasoning for termination, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: Reasoning for termination uses a large language model to assess accumulated gist memory against the original query, explain answerability, and end retrieval iterations when the query is answerable.

l: query re-writing, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: Query re-writing uses the original query, accumulated gist memory, and previous reasoning output to generate an updated next query, which is passed to the retriever when another iteration is required.

l: after termination, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: After termination, each proximal triple in the final gist memory is linked to passages; linked and iteration-retrieved passages are combined using Reciprocal Rank Fusion into a final ranked list.

l: base retriever, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: returns passage [for the input query] The base retriever returns an initial list of passages for the input query. This list is used by knowledge synchronisation to identify proximal triples and by Synchronised Graph Expansion as the initial passage set.

l: Reciprocal Rank Fusion, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines rankings from retrieval sources, merging expanded and initial passages and BM25 with Sentence-BERT, then producing GEAR's final ranking across linked and iteration-level passages.

l: answerability assessment, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: determines input query [answerability given the evidence in gist memory] Answerability assessment determines whether the accumulated gist memory contains sufficient evidence to answer the original question. When the query is answerable, GEAR concludes its iterative retrieval process.

l: GPT-4o mini, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: GPT-4o mini is a large language model used for all LLM-requiring methods and corresponding triple extraction, with temperature set to 0.

l: multi-step retrieval methods, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: The framework’s primary contribution is retrieval, evaluated with Recall@5, Recall@10, and Recall@15 for single- and multi-step retrievers; its agent-based GEAR approach leads results across three datasets, with especially strong gains on MuSiQue.

l: Recall@k, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: Recall@k measures retrieval performance as the percentage of questions whose correct entries appear within the top 5, 10, or 15 retrieved passages, computed cumulatively each iteration. It is used to compare recall ranks: Diverse Triple Beam Search improves it across datasets, while GEAR shows stronger mean or median recall in specified multi-hop settings.

l: Hybrid + SyncGE, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: Hybrid + SyncGE is a single-step retrieval method whose Diverse Triple Beam Search improves recall across MuSiQue, 2Wiki, and HotpotQA. It achieves state-of-the-art retrieval on MuSiQue and HotpotQA, surpassing HippoRAG by up to 9.8% R@15 on MuSiQue, while using fewer tokens than HippoRAG w/ IRCoT; however, its cited single-iteration R@15 is substantially lower.

l: HippoRAG w/ IRCoT, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: HippoRAG w/ IRCoT is used as a multi-step retrieval comparison. On MuSiQue, GEAR shows a 21% relative improvement in R@15 and a 37% relative improvement in both EM and F1 compared with HippoRAG w/ IRCoT. HippoRAG w/ IRCoT generally requires at least two iterations to reach maximum performance and uses more LLM tokens than GEAR. GEAR has a higher mean recall on 2-hop questions and outperforms its median performance across both 3-hop subdivisions, while the two methods have similar interquartile ranges on 2-hop questions.

l: single-step retrieval, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: SyncGE contributes to state-of-the-art performance in single-step retrieval. Hybrid + SyncGE achieves state-of-the-art results on both MuSiQue and HotpotQA and outperforms HippoRAG in many configurations.

l: retrieval recall, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: correlates_with question answering performance [positively] The analysis reports a positive correlation between retrieval recall and question answering performance. On MuSiQue, GEAR has a 21% relative improvement in R@15 over HippoRAG w/ IRCoT.

l: retrieval performance, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: Retrieval performance improves with both graph expansion variants across all evaluated datasets. GEAR reaches strong retrieval performance in one iteration on MuSiQue and performs particularly well on low-to-moderate-complexity questions.

l: LLM token utilisation, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: GEAR uses fewer LLM tokens than HippoRAG w/ IRCoT even in a single iteration, and the difference increases as the number of iterations grows. SyncGE outperforms a more LLM-heavy solution on MuSiQue while using almost 2.9 million fewer tokens.

l: this paper, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: This paper scopes retrieval through a graph of triples bridging corresponding passages. It demonstrates the effectiveness of graph expansion and GEAR, using gist memory and a reasoner as agent components, while citing work on entity disambiguation, graph completion, inference, and validated practices. It ends by identifying components for future refinement.

l: graph construction methods, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: Graph construction methods could become more sophisticated to address entity disambiguation and knowledge graph completion, yielding further improvements.

l: scoring function, GEAR: Graph-enhanced Agent for Retrieval-augmented Generation
s: is_used_in diverse triple beam search The scoring function in the diverse triple beam search uses a dense embedding model. It could instead be formulated as a natural language inference task.

l: RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems, by Robert Friel, Masha Belyi, and Atindriyo Sanyal of Galileo Technologies Inc., presents a benchmark and evaluation framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). RAG combines document retrieval with a Large Language Model, but generated answers can still hallucinate or fail to use relevant retrieved evidence. The paper argues that automated, granular evaluation is needed for both retrievers and response generators. It introduces RAGBench, a roughly 100k-example collection standardized from 12 real-world academic and industry datasets. Its five broad domains are biomedical research, general knowledge, legal contracts, customer support, and finance; tasks include question answering, numerical reasoning over tables and text, and multi-document retrieval and reasoning. Components have non-overlapping train, validation, and test splits and vary in contexts, lengths, generators, and retrieval setups. The paper then defines TRACe, which evaluates Context Relevance, Context Utilization, Adherence, and Completeness. Relevance asks how much retrieved context pertains to the query; utilization asks how much is used in the answer; completeness measures whether relevant information is incorporated; and adherence tests whether the answer is grounded in context rather than hallucinated. GPT-4 produces relevance, utilization, and adherence labels, with completeness derived from span-level annotations. Post-processing uses explanations, redundancy, consistency checks, and re-annotation. Validation against DelucionQA human judgments reports high agreement, while hallucination rates differ substantially across datasets. A case study evaluates 32 simulated RAG systems using RAGTruth queries, different retrievers, document counts, models, and prompts. GPT-4o and chain-of-thought prompting generally reduce hallucinations and improve utilization and completeness. FAISS tends to yield higher relevance than TF-IDF, and retrieving two documents generally performs better than four. Estimating relevance remains especially difficult because semantically related material may lack the precise information needed. Finally, the authors compare GPT-3.5-judge, RAGAS, TruLens, and a fine-tuned DeBERTa-v3-Large evaluator. A 400M-parameter fine-tuned DeBERTa model outperforms few-shot LLM judges in many settings and competes with commercial systems, though a substantial gap from ground truth remains. The paper releases RAGBench data on Hugging Face and inference and evaluation code on GitHub, framing the benchmark and TRACe as resources for stronger, more explainable RAG evaluation.

l: RAGBench, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: RAGBench is an explainable, comprehensive, large-scale benchmark dataset for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems. It contains 100k real-world RAG examples across five source domains, biomedical research, general knowledge, legal contracts, customer support, and finance, and is intended to train and benchmark powerful RAG evaluation models. Its central contribution is explainable labeling for holistic evaluation and actionable feedback: annotations cover context relevance, answer faithfulness or adherence, context utilization, and answer completeness, including utilization and completeness as new evaluation metrics. These labels, automatically generated with an LLM and reported to correlate highly with human judgments, support more precise diagnosis of RAG systems’ strengths and weaknesses and iterative improvement of production applications. The benchmark unfolds by standardizing 12 publicly released academic and industry component datasets into a consistent retrieval-augmented generation format: PubMedQA, CovidQA-RAG, HotpotQA, MS Marco, HAGRID, ExpertQA, DelucionQA, EManual, TechQA, FinQA, TAT-QA, and CUAD. It reframes datasets as RAG tasks by retrieving or supplying context and generating responses, while retaining existing ExpertQA responses. Construction varies domains, document counts, context lengths from 100 to 11k tokens, and response-generation models. It uses OpenAI embeddings and FAISS for PQA-U context retrieval, and generates responses with GPT-3.5 and Claude 3 Haiku at temperature 1.0. The resulting data are divided into non-overlapping train, validation, and test splits; component datasets include 1% to 20% hallucinated responses. RAGBench is used to assess retriever relevance, response adherence, and response completeness, including benchmarking LLM evaluators and training and testing a fine-tuned DeBERTa judge. Released as a labeled dataset on Hugging Face, with inference and evaluation code on GitHub, it provides standardized benchmarks and methodologies intended to advance more mature RAG evaluation systems.

l: RAG, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: RAG is a system architecture and architectural pattern for bringing domain-specific knowledge into user-facing chat and dialogue applications powered by Large Language Models. It combines a retriever, which queries relevant documents from an in-domain corpus, with a generator that uses those documents and the user query to produce an informed response. Its central purpose is to ground models in factual information and improve knowledge-intensive NLP tasks, including open-domain question answering. Retrieved documents are generally semantically related to the query, but the records stress that semantic similarity alone does not prove that context is relevant for answering it. RAG is increasingly used in real-world applications and develops through iterative improvement of RAG models. Evaluation is a major concern: it examines retrieved context, generated answers, hallucinations, attribution, adherence, relevance, utilization, completeness, and system-level correctness. RAGTruth provides a hallucination corpus; RAGAs and ARES evaluate it; CRAG and Chinese domain-specific DomainRAG are benchmarks; and validation data are sampled from KILT, including Natural Questions, HotpotQA, FEVER, and Wizards of Wikipedia. RAGBench standardizes 12 component datasets into the RAG format, varying document count, context length, source domain, and response-generation model to represent real-world scenarios. Its simulated systems retrieve context and generate responses, using TF-IDF or FAISS retrieval, different context and prompt settings, and GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 or GPT-4o. The work culminates in a goal of more precise, actionable evaluation for real-world RAG systems.

l: RAG, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: RAG, or retrieval-augmented generation, is a system/technology with two components: a document retriever and a downstream Large Language Models response-generation component. It queries a domain-specific corpus for context relevant to an input query, then generates a response from the query and retrieved context. It can boost knowledge-intensive tasks through additional context, but production settings can include hallucinations. Its design varies by retriever, retrieved-document number, generation model, context format and length, and generation prompt, so application-specific optimization is complex and costly and requires balancing accuracy and efficiency. Evaluation is challenging because unified criteria and annotated datasets are lacking. TRACe evaluates relevance, utilization, adherence, and completeness: retrievers should return necessary information without superfluous data, while generators should rely strictly on context. In simulated systems, retriever configuration affects relevance, and LLM and prompt choices affect utilization, hallucinations, and completeness. Benchmarks and methodologies provide insights into strengths and weaknesses for iterative improvement.

l: large language models, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: Large language models are pre-trained generative models that power chat applications, generating responses from queries and, in retrieval-augmented systems, retrieved context. They show strong reasoning and conversation but struggle with out-of-domain, knowledge-intensive questions without retrieval support. Their development and use are accompanied by benchmarking and evaluation for factuality, hallucination, instruction following, attribution, reasoning, and model judging.

l: retriever, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: Retriever queries domain-specific corpora for context relevant to an input query. Its key measure is Context Relevance, the average relevance of retrieved documents per query. Evaluations compare sparse TF-IDF and dense retrievers; inefficient retrieval can return excessive information, raising costs and potentially harming response quality.

l: TRACe, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: TRACe is a RAG evaluation framework for RAG systems, formalized with explainable and actionable metrics applicable across RAG domains. It standardizes evaluation through a consistent, systematic approach to measuring performance across related dimensions. Its four metrics are Utilization, Relevance or Context Relevance, Adherence, and Completeness. It evaluates retrievers and response generators through retrieval efficiency, context use, incorporation of relevant information, and response grounding. TRACe is evaluated in a case study of different RAG configurations, where Relevance, Utilization, and Adherence are measured and metrics are predicted by LLM-based and fine-tuned judges. Post-processing for Adherence appears to improve relevance and utilization label quality and stability. It is proposed for adoption with RAGBench.

l: RAG evaluation metrics, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: are_applicable_to RAG systems [across all RAG domains] RAG evaluation metrics are provided through the TRACe framework, which makes them explainable and actionable across RAG domains.

l: RoBERTa, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: is_a finetuned model [used on the RAG evaluation task] A finetuned RoBERTa model outperforms LLM-based RAG evaluation methods in the reported RAG evaluation benchmarking, with LLM-based methods struggling to compete.

l: RAG evaluation, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: RAG evaluation is an automated evaluation task for comparing and tuning RAG system configurations. It matters because unified criteria and annotated datasets are lacking, while evaluation spans relevance, faithfulness, hallucination, attribution, adherence, and completeness. It unfolds from identifying fragmented benchmarks and datasets to presenting RAGBench and TRACe, while noting LLM-based methods lag a finetuned RoBERTa model.

l: Hugging Face, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: Hugging Face hosts the RAGBench dataset. Its model card and documentation are referenced for further information.

l: hallucinations, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: Hallucinations are non-adherent or insufficiently grounded response content in RAG systems and AI legal research tools. They matter because production RAG systems remain prone to them when generator models struggle to retrieve relevant information from provided context. Under the annotation scheme, partially supported sentences count as hallucinations; a response is labeled Hallucinated when it contains a Conflicted or Neither sentence, though examples with Neither annotations are removed for analysis because filler and missing-information claims are generally grounded. HaluEval evaluates them. In RAGBench, they occur in 1% to 20% of component-dataset responses, highest in ExpertQA, CovidQA, and MS Marco and lowest in Cuad, FinQA, and TAT-QA. GPT-4o with chain-of-thought has the lowest amount, while GPT-3.5 increases under it.

l: RAGAS, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: RAGAS is an automated RAG evaluation system using zero-shot LLM prompts to predict curated metrics. It defines and evaluates context relevance, answer relevance, and faithfulness. In its case study, it uses few-shot GPT-3.5 prompts with a curated prompt to measure context relevance and answer groundedness, called Adherence, while not evaluating Utilization in the reported comparison.

l: TruLens, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: TruLens is an automated RAG evaluation system using zero-shot LLM prompts to predict curated metrics. It measures Context Relevance and answer faithfulness as Adherence; in the reported comparison, it does not evaluate Utilization.

l: RAGTruth, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: RAGTruth is a small RAG evaluation benchmark and hallucination detection dataset, supplying labeled hallucinations, 100 queries, and 2,512 context chunks for a case study.

l: Context Relevance, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: Context Relevance is a retriever quality metric for evaluating documents retrieved by a RAG system with respect to an input query. It measures the fraction of retrieved context that is relevant, identifying document sentences or documents that contain useful, necessary information for answering the question; removing such documents would affect answerability. It is calculated for individual context documents and can be aggregated over all documents in an example. Low Context Relevance indicates retriever inefficiency. Evaluation requires deriving the correct answer and then determining which context supports it, making it generally harder to predict than Utilization. RAGAS evaluates it with an LLM judge, while ARES fine-tunes smaller NLI models. In DelucionQA(40), GPT-4 span-level labels reached F1 0.76 and accuracy 0.78 against human judgements. Across sampled examples, average scores rank simulated RAG systems: binary relevance rankings show high Kendall’s tau, whereas continuous scores may agree less because they reflect retrieved-context length differences.

l: answer relevance, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: Answer relevance evaluates generative-model response quality; RAGAS assesses it with an LLM judge, while ARES predicts it using fine-tuned smaller NLI models.

l: answer faithfullness, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: Answer faithfulness is a metric evaluating generative-model response quality, used in RAGBench and studied in open-domain conversational question answering. It is evaluated by RAGAS with an LLM judge and by ARES using fine-tuned smaller NLI models.

l: Context Utilization, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: Context Utilization is a RAG evaluation and generator quality metric, introduced in RAGBench and TRACe to give a granular, actionable view of RAG performance. It measures, at the example level across context documents, the fraction of retrieved context the generator uses to produce a response. It is assessed by semantic comparison of context and response, including labels of utilized substrings. Low Utilization with low Relevance suggests a greedy retriever; low Utilization alone suggests a weak generator. On DelucionQA(40), GPT-4 span-level labels achieved 0.92 F1 and 0.94 accuracy against human judgements.

l: response completeness, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: is_a RAG evaluation metric [new] Answer completeness is introduced as a new metric in RAGBench. It is intended to provide a more granular and actionable description of overall RAG system performance.

l: DeBERTa-large, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: DeBERTa-large is a 400M-parameter model fine-tuned on RAGBench that outperforms few-shot LLM judges, motivating future RAG evaluation and benchmark improvement.

l: DelucionQA, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: DelucionQA is a human-annotated, RAG-specific hallucination-detection benchmark in customer support. It is a curated collection of queries about operating the 2023 Gladiator, grounded in Jeep’s Gladiator User Manual. The dataset has 913 unique questions and 1,046 context passages; its questions are described as crowd-sourced and as initially generated by large language models. RAGBench builds a vector database from the passages, retrieves up to three documents per question with text-embedding-ada-002, and generates responses with various LLMs. Humans annotate contextual support and hallucination at example and span levels, with 421 annotated examples noted as remaining examples handled by an LLM annotator. The benchmark validates metric formulations and labeling, including comparison of GPT-4 and human annotations on its test split and granular Relevance and Utilization validation using the randomly sampled DelucionQA(40) subset.

l: GPT-3.5, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: GPT-3.5 is a response-generator LLM identified as gpt-3.5-0125, with a 16k-token context limit. It generates responses for most component datasets but not CUAD, whose contexts exceed that limit. It also serves as a judge and evaluator; it hallucinates more than GPT-4o, especially with chain-of-thought prompting.

l: Adherence, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: Adherence is a generator quality metric that detects hallucinations in RAG responses by measuring whether a response is grounded in its provided context. Also called answer faithfullness, groundednes, or attribution in the literature, it requires every response part to be supported. At the example level, it is a boolean: all response sentences must be supported; annotations also exist at response, sentence, span, and token levels. Supported tokens enable granular evaluation, while disagreements between response- and sentence-level assessments flag examples for re-annotation. Extra annotation measures can improve relevance, utilization, quality, and stability. In reported evaluation on DelucionQA, GPT-4 labels achieved high example- and span-level F1 and accuracy. It can also be estimated on response tokens by a fine-tuned DeBERTa model.

l: hallucination detection, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: Hallucination detection is a RAG evaluation focus, addressed by datasets, NLI models, and fine-tuned LLM judges. It is evaluated as response-level classification with AUROC; a RAGBench-trained NLI model outperforms LLM judges, while fine-tuned DeBERTa performs competitively across test splits.

l: LLM Judges, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: LLM Judges are an automated RAG evaluation approach and LLM evaluator. They use prompted models such as GPT-3.5 to assess context relevance, answer relevance, faithfulness, hallucination, and utilization. Benchmarks compare zero-shot and framework-based judges with fine-tuned models; a RAGBench-trained NLI model outperforms fine-tuned judges for hallucination and attribution detection.

l: Natural Language Inference, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: is_a RAG evaluation [methodological basis for NLI models] Natural Language Inference measures the degree of entailment between a premise and a hypothesis. The unit explains that this capability has been repurposed to evaluate response attribution in RAG settings.

l: NLI models, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: NLI models measure entailment between premise and hypothesis, supporting RAG hallucination detection, response attribution, and relevance or faithfulness evaluation; fine-tuning with RAGBench performs well on newly proposed RAG evaluation metrics.

l: attribution, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: Attribution links generated answers to supporting sources and evaluates evidential support, spanning attributed question answering, citation generation, collaborative work, and automatic LLM evaluation.

l: DeBERTa-v3-Large, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: DeBERTa-v3-Large is a 400M-parameter NLI model fine-tuned on RAGBench for RAG evaluation. It uses separate prediction heads on context tokens for Context Relevance and Utilization and on response tokens for Adherence; sentence-level annotations are broadcast to tokens during training, and relevant, utilized, and adherent spans are predicted at a 0.5 threshold. It is trained for three epochs on a Google Cloud Platform A-100 GPU instance, with distinct initial learning rates for base layers and heads, warmup, and linear decay. Across RAGBench domain subsets, it performs competitively with billion-parameter LLM judges and commercial RAG evaluation systems, and is reported to outperform LLM judges in hallucination and attribution detection.

l: RAG evaluation benchmarks, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: is_a RAG evaluation [benchmarks] RAG evaluation benchmarks are presented as necessary for comparing automated RAG evaluation approaches. The unit identifies the lack of established benchmarks as a difficulty and presents RAGBench as an effort to address it.

l: PubMedQA, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: PubMedQA is a biomedical research collection of PubMed research abstracts paired with automatically generated yes/no/maybe questions derived from article titles. It includes PQA-L, PQA-U, and PQA-A, and requires retrieval and reasoning across multiple context documents. In RAGBench, PQA-U is reframed with segmented chunks, retrieval from a 200k-entry vector database, and generated responses.

l: CovidQA-RAG, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: CovidQA-RAG is a biomedical research dataset combining 2k expert-annotated COVID-QA questions with a vector database of 250,000 100-word passages. It embeds questions and passages, retrieves up to N passages through FAISS, then generates LLM RAG responses requiring multi-document retrieval and reasoning. Its 16% hallucination rate is among RAGBench’s highest.

l: HotpotQA, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: HotpotQA is a crowd-sourced question-answer dataset for general knowledge, using Wikipedia contexts and questions. It contains 113K question-answer pairs and emphasizes retrieval and multi-hop reasoning across multiple documents. In RAGBench, its dev-distractor split is sampled, contexts reduced to four documents while retaining the response document, and LLM responses generated.

l: MS Marco, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: MS Marco is an open-domain question-answering dataset of general-knowledge web pages and real-world Bing user queries. It provides ten Bing-retrieved passages per question. RAGBench samples its train, validation, and test splits, replaces human answers with LLM-generated responses, and reports a 13% hallucination rate.

l: CUAD, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: CUAD is a collection of 510 commercial legal contracts from EDGAR, with 21k expert-annotated questions, responses, and relevant contract portions. It supplies legal-contract documents and expert-composed questions to RAGBench. Its up-to-11k-token, contract-specific contexts create a specialized long-context setting; RAGBench uses one contract, samples five questions, and generates LLM responses, with about a 1% hallucination rate.

l: EManual, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: EManual is a customer-support dataset in RAGBench built from a TV manual and annotator-written questions. It centers on 659 questions about a Samsung Smart TV and remote and 261 manual chunks, which are embedded, retrieved as up to three contexts per question, and used to generate responses.

l: TechQA, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: TechQA is a collection of 1.4k real-world customer-support questions from IBMDeveloper and DeveloperWorks, paired with technical-support documents from technotes and tech forums. It includes unanswerable cases; RAGBench uses its splits, samples ten documents per question while retaining applicable answer documents, and generates LLM responses.

l: FinQA, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: FinQA is a finance QA dataset built from financial report passages, earnings reports, and expert-composed questions. It contains 8,281 question-answer pairs requiring numerical reasoning across unstructured text and tables. RAGBench retains its train, validation, and test splits, generates two LLM responses per example, and reports about a 1% hallucination rate.

l: TAT-QA, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: TAT-QA is a financial QA dataset built from 500 annual financial reports sourced from annualreports.com and expert-composed questions. It requires numerical reasoning across tables and text, contributes finance data to RAGBench, and has about a 1% hallucination rate there; RAGBench uses its full dataset to generate new LLM responses.

l: ExpertQA, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: ExpertQA is a general-knowledge collection of domain-expert-curated questions in science, arts, and law, with expert-curated relevant passages and original LLM-generated responses. Sourced through Google search and expert-composed questions, it is used directly by RAGBench; its 12% hallucination rate is among RAGBench’s highest.

l: HAGRID, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: HAGRID is a general-knowledge dataset built on MIRACL, using Wikipedia context and expert-composed questions. Relevant documents are passed to an LLM to produce responses; because its original data already contains LLM-generated responses, RAGBench uses them directly.

l: Claude 3 Haiku, RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
s: is_a response generator model Claude 3 Haiku is used to generate one of two responses per input for most component datasets. It is the only response-generation model used for CUAD because CUAD's contexts are too long for GPT-3.5's 16k-token limit.
